Furthermore, for every {{mvar|r}} in {{mvar|R}}, right (or left) multiplication by {{mvar|r}} gives rise to a morphism of {{math|(''R'', +)}}, by right (or left) distributivity. Let {{math|1=''A'' = (''R'', +)}}. Consider those [[endomorphism]]s of {{mvar|A}}, that "factor through" right (or left) multiplication of {{mvar|R}}. In other words, let {{math|End{{sub|''R''}}(''A'')}} be the set of all morphisms {{mvar|m}} of {{mvar|A}}, having the property that {{math|1=''m''(''r'' ⋅ ''x'') = ''r'' ⋅ ''m''(''x'')}}. It was seen that every {{mvar|r}} in {{mvar|R}} gives rise to a morphism of {{mvar|A}}: right multiplication by {{mvar|r}}. It is in fact true that this association of any element of {{mvar|R}}, to a morphism of {{mvar|A}}, as a function from {{mvar|R}} to {{math|End{{sub|''R''}}(''A'')}}, is an isomorphism of rings. In this sense, therefore, any ring can be viewed as the endomorphism ring of some abelian {{mvar|X}}-group (by {{mvar|X}}-group, it is meant a group with {{mvar|X}} being its [[Group with operators|set of operators]]).{{sfnp|Jacobson|2009|p=162|loc=Theorem 3.2|ps=}} In essence, the most general form of a ring, is the endomorphism group of some abelian {{mvar|X}}-group.

Any ring can be seen as a [[preadditive category]] with a single object. It is therefore natural to consider arbitrary preadditive categories to be generalizations of rings. And indeed, many definitions and theorems originally given for rings can be translated to this more general context. [[Additive functor]]s between preadditive categories generalize the concept of ring homomorphism, and ideals in additive categories can be defined as sets of [[morphism]]s closed under addition and under composition with arbitrary morphisms.

== Generalization ==
Algebraists have defined structures more general than rings by weakening or dropping some of ring axioms.

=== Rng ===
A [[rng (algebra)|rng]] is the same as a ring, except that the existence of a multiplicative identity is not assumed.{{sfnp|Jacobson|2009|ps=}}

=== Nonassociative ring ===
A [[nonassociative ring]] is an algebraic structure that satisfies all of the ring axioms except the associative property and the existence of a multiplicative identity. A notable example is a [[Lie algebra]]. There exists some structure theory<!-- developed by Jacobson? --> for such algebras that generalizes the analogous results for Lie algebras and associative algebras.{{citation needed|date=November 2013}}

=== Semiring ===
A [[semiring]] (sometimes ''rig'') is obtained by weakening the assumption that {{math|(''R'', +)}} is an abelian group to the assumption that {{math|(''R'', +)}} is a commutative monoid, and adding the axiom that {{math|1=0 ⋅ ''a'' = ''a'' ⋅ 0 = 0}} for all ''a'' in {{mvar|R}} (since it no longer follows from the other axioms).

Examples:
* the non-negative integers <math>\{0,1,2,\ldots\}</math> with ordinary addition and multiplication;
* the [[tropical semiring]].

== Other ring-like objects ==

=== Ring object in a category ===
Let {{mvar|C}} be a category with finite [[Product (category theory)|products]]. Let pt denote a [[terminal object]] of {{mvar|C}} (an empty product). A '''ring object''' in {{mvar|C}} is an object {{mvar|R}} equipped with morphisms <math>R \times R\;\stackrel{a}\to\,R</math> (addition), <math>R \times R\;\stackrel{m}\to\,R</math> (multiplication), <math>\operatorname{pt}\stackrel{0}\to\,R</math> (additive identity), <math>R\;\stackrel{i}\to\,R</math> (additive inverse), and <math>\operatorname{pt}\stackrel{1}\to\,R</math> (multiplicative identity) satisfying the usual ring axioms. Equivalently, a ring object is an object {{mvar|R}} equipped with a factorization of its functor of points <math>h_R = \operatorname{Hom}(-,R) : C^{\operatorname{op}} \to \mathbf{Sets}</math> through the category of rings: <math>C^{\operatorname{op}} \to \mathbf{Rings} \stackrel{\textrm{forgetful}}\longrightarrow \mathbf{Sets}.</math>

=== Ring scheme ===
In algebraic geometry, a '''ring scheme''' over a base [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] {{mvar|S}} is a ring object in the category of {{mvar|S}}-schemes. One example is the ring scheme {{math|W{{sub|''n''}}}} over {{tmath|\operatorname{Spec} \Z}}, which for any commutative ring {{mvar|A}} returns the ring {{math|W{{sub|''n''}}(''A'')}} of {{mvar|p}}-isotypic [[Witt vector]]s of length {{mvar|n}} over {{mvar|A}}.<ref>Serre, p.&nbsp;44</ref>

=== Ring spectrum ===
In [[algebraic topology]], a [[ring spectrum]] is a [[spectrum (topology)|spectrum]] {{mvar|X}} together with a multiplication <math>\mu : X \wedge X \to X</math> and a unit map {{math|''S'' → ''X''}} from the [[sphere spectrum]] {{mvar|S}}, such that the ring axiom diagrams commute up to [[homotopy]]. In practice, it is common to define a ring spectrum as a [[monoid object]] in a good category of spectra such as the category of [[symmetric spectrum|symmetric spectra]].
